scenes.narration: Three straight cuts. How many pieces can you make? Six is easy if every cut passes through the center. But slide the last cut away from that crossing. A tiny seventh piece appears. Keep the pizza flat. No stacking or moving pieces between cuts. How does one extra piece sneak in? Follow the last cut from one edge to the other. Each old line it crosses takes it into a new region. With two distinct crossings, the blade passes through three regions. It splits each one in two, adding three pieces. If all the lines meet at one point, those crossings merge. We lose one of the regions the new cut could split. Now try a fourth cut. Make it cross all three old cuts, at three different points inside the pizza. Those crossings divide the new cut into four sections. Four sections split four old regions. Seven becomes eleven. That is the maximum. A fourth straight line cannot cross each of three old straight lines more than once. For the next cut, predict the biggest increase. Five old-region sections means five extra pieces. Eleven becomes sixteen. The numbers come from new regions crossed, not from counting slices around the center.
